title: Counting Which Genes a Cell Uses
endLine: Sequencing RNA counts which genes each cell uses right now.

scenes.tts: Every cell carries almost the same genome, so which genes are active? What makes a keratinocyte, a skin cell, differ from a macrophage, an immune cell, is which genes it transcribes. Transcription copies a stretch of DNA into RNA. Transcription factors and chromatin hold each cell's pattern in place. Single-cell RNA sequencing is one way to read that pattern.

scenes.visual: Full-frame schematic cross-section of living tissue showing packed cells, focusing on a flat keratinocyte beside an amoeboid macrophage; both contain identical schematic genome bars (no molecular structures). Before narration names them, glowing RNA ribbons drift out from different bands on each genome bar, labelled "Keratinocyte" and "Macrophage" (schematic). Slow ambient drift continues throughout.

scenes.visual: The same schematic tissue cross-section dims slightly while its glowing RNA ribbons keep drifting upward. The title "Counting Which Genes a Cell Uses" fades in large at full contrast, holds briefly, then clears as the tissue sharpens again.

scenes.tts: First, the tissue is separated into single cells, usually with enzymes. Each captured RNA is copied into DNA so it can be sequenced. Before cells are mixed, every copy from one cell gets the same cell barcode. That barcode is a short sequence tag marking its cell of origin.
scenes.caption: First, the tissue is separated into single cells, usually with enzymes. Each captured RNA is copied into DNA so it can be sequenced. Before cells are mixed, every copy from one cell gets the same cell barcode. That barcode is a short sequence tag marking its cell of origin.
scenes.visual: In the same schematic tissue view, gentle enzyme pulses drift across and separate the packed cells so the keratinocyte and macrophage float apart. Inside each separated cell, glowing RNA ribbons transform into sturdier schematic DNA strips (no molecular structures). A bright teal end-tag snaps onto every DNA strip in the keratinocyte, and an amber end-tag snaps onto every strip in the macrophage, labelled "Cell barcode (schematic)".
scenes.narration: First, the tissue is separated into single cells, usually with enzymes. Each captured RNA is copied into DNA so it can be sequenced. Before cells are mixed, every copy from one cell gets the same cell barcode. That barcode is a short sequence tag marking its cell of origin.

scenes.tts: Next, the pooled DNA is sequenced together. Cell barcodes sort every read back to its starting cell. Counts fill a count matrix: one row per gene, one column per sampled cell. Each entry counts reads, or molecules when each copy carries a unique molecular identifier. Sequencing RNA counts which genes each cell uses right now.

scenes.visual: Teal and amber barcoded DNA strips pour from the separated cells into one mixed stream flowing through a schematic sequencer gate. Emerging reads sort themselves by tag colour into columns of a growing grid labelled "Count matrix (schematic)", with gene rows along the left and sampled cell columns across the top. Grid boxes brighten with schematic count bars as entries fill in.

scenes.tts: A count matrix holds many genes across many cells, so software groups cells with similar expression profiles. Each group is a cluster. Comparing a cluster's genes with known profiles to propose an identity is annotation. Notice the word propose. Counts can still mislead.

scenes.visual: Columns lift from the schematic count matrix and shrink into coloured dots on a schematic scatter map. Dots with matching expression profiles drift together into two tight groups labelled "Cluster (schematic)" (teal dots on one side, amber dots on the other). Known reference profiles glide beside each cluster to propose "Keratinocyte?" and "Macrophage?", labelled "Annotation".

scenes.tts: Suppose you want the genes that nerve growth factor, N G F, controls in sympathetic neurons of living animals. Those neurons sit in groups called ganglia. Here is the catch: without N G F, the neurons die. If you compare RNA from normal ganglia and ganglia lacking N G F, what misleads your counts?
scenes.caption: Suppose you want the genes that nerve growth factor, NGF, controls in sympathetic neurons of living animals. Those neurons sit in groups called ganglia. Here is the catch: without NGF, the neurons die. If you compare RNA from normal ganglia and ganglia lacking NGF, what misleads your counts?
scenes.visual: Carrying the same schematic cell style, two side-by-side groups of sympathetic neurons appear, labelled "Ganglion + NGF" and "Ganglion, no NGF" (schematic). On the right, neurons dim and fade away as NGF leaves, while an empty schematic count column drops beside them. A large, high-contrast question appears above: "What misleads this RNA comparison?"
scenes.narration: Suppose you want the genes that nerve growth factor, NGF, controls in sympathetic neurons of living animals. Those neurons sit in groups called ganglia. Here is the catch: without NGF, the neurons die. If you compare RNA from normal ganglia and ganglia lacking NGF, what misleads your counts?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause: the question "What misleads this RNA comparison?" remains on screen above the two schematic ganglia—full living neurons on the left and fading neurons on the right—while their paired schematic count columns pulse gently.

scenes.tts: Without living neurons, every neuron gene drops together. Your counts measure cell loss, not which genes N G F controls. So both groups must keep living neurons. A second limit is time. An RNA profile is a snapshot of active genes. A hidden fate bias, a leaning toward one future cell type, can escape it.

scenes.visual: On the right schematic ganglion, the entire count column collapses together and is marked "Cell loss, not NGF". A protective outline then keeps the right ganglion's neurons intact while NGF leaves, restoring a fair schematic comparison. Next, a camera-shutter frame flashes around one schematic cell, showing active RNA bars now while two diverging future paths stay unlit outside the frame.
scenes.narration: Without living neurons, every neuron gene drops together. Your counts measure cell loss, not which genes NGF controls. So both groups must keep living neurons. A second limit is time. An RNA profile is a snapshot of active genes. A hidden fate bias, a leaning toward one future cell type, can escape it.

scenes.tts: That control worked in living animals. Deppmann, Ginty and colleagues used mice lacking Bax, a protein these neurons need to die. Without Bax, sympathetic neurons survive without N G F. They compared those ganglia with ganglia lacking both Bax and N G F. That gave N G F dependent genes: transcription factors, synaptic genes, metabolism, cell size, and axon growth.
scenes.caption: That control worked in living animals. Deppmann, Ginty and colleagues used mice lacking Bax, a protein these neurons need to die. Without Bax, sympathetic neurons survive without NGF. They compared those ganglia with ganglia lacking both Bax and NGF. That gave NGF-dependent genes: transcription factors, synaptic genes, metabolism, cell size, and axon growth.
scenes.visual: Side-by-side schematic ganglia both stay full of living neurons: left labelled "Lacking Bax", right labelled "Lacking Bax and NGF", with source tag "Deppmann, Ginty and colleagues". Comparing their schematic count columns highlights four groups of gene rows that drop on the right (NGF-dependent): "Transcription factors", "Synaptic genes", "Metabolism & cell size", and "Axon growth".
scenes.narration: That control worked in living animals. Deppmann, Ginty and colleagues used mice lacking Bax, a protein these neurons need to die. scenes.tts: A snapshot can also miss things. Weinreb, Klein, Camargo and colleagues gave mouse blood progenitors, the parent cells of blood, inherited DNA barcodes expressed as RNA. They sequenced some cells early and followed their sisters' progeny. Sister cells shared fate biases that the RNA profiles had not detected. RNA counts capture active genes now, not a cell's whole story.

scenes.visual: In the same schematic cell world, a dividing mouse blood progenitor passes a glowing inherited barcode ring to two sister cells, tagged "Weinreb, Klein, Camargo and colleagues" (schematic). One sister enters the schematic sequencer early—yielding a nearly flat schematic count column—while the other sister divides into progeny drifting clearly toward one blood fate. Matching fate glows on both sisters reveal the bias the early RNA profile missed.
